verdict.root_cause: Cart's backing store is reachable and fast but holds at least one payload that cart cannot decode: every cart error line in the window is the identical FailedPrecondition carrying a Google.Protobuf.InvalidProtocolBufferException reporting that the input ended in the middle of a field [tr_871968a1ced8]. Traces confirm the failure is a data-shape fault above the storage call rather than a storage outage or slowness — the Redis HGET child span still completes in sub-millisecond time inside failing traces, and the error status originates at the cart handler span [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. Checkout is a victim, not a cause: every failing checkout trace aborts at its first downstream hop, CartService/GetCart, before currency, product-catalog, shipping, payment, email or the orders publish are ever invoked, and checkout/frontend/frontend-proxy spans merely re-wrap the cart status with negligible self time [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. Onset is bounded to just before 21:56:30Z, with failures continuing unbroken to the window edge [tr_871968a1ced8], and no deploy, config edit or flag flip is recorded for either checkout [tr_4ef11f576ced] or cart [tr_b83043db5026] in the window the change log actually covered.
verdict.reasoning: Two independent signals converge on the same mechanism. The cart log shows a single, byte-identical failure signature — a protobuf parse exception on data already received — which requires a successful connection and response from the store, explicitly excluding connectivity, auth and timeout failures [tr_871968a1ced8]. The trace evidence puts the error status at the cart handler span while the Redis read beneath it succeeds in 0.2-0.7ms, and rules out latency as the terminal condition because failing traces fail fast with an explicit FailedPrecondition rather than an elapsed deadline [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. That is the definition of a store that is healthy and whose contents cannot be read. Blame is directed at cart rather than checkout because checkout's own logs are entirely absent [tr_a3d27276183e] and its traces show it doing nothing wrong — it propagates a status it received [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. The write path (EmptyCart, HMSET/EXPIRE) completes normally; only the GetCart read path errors [tr_45a6a0243e5f], consistent with a bad payload already resident in storage rather than an ongoing write fault. Change evidence is weakly exculpatory at best: both change queries ran from onset forward for ~24h and did not cover the hours preceding 21:56 [tr_4ef11f576ced, tr_b83043db5026], so 'no change' is an answer about the wrong window. The low aggregate error ratios on both services [tr_6a4cad08a919, tr_7ba8e797a1a7] do not contradict this — the ratios are service-wide and operation-blind, and only the subset of sessions whose stored cart is corrupt will fail, which matches the trace finding that the failures cluster in the user_checkout_multi scenario while user_checkout_single traces succeed end to end. The fix is to purge or restore the unreadable cart entries; a restart of cart will not change bytes sitting in the store, and there is no change to revert.
open_questions: Whether the corruption is confined to a small set of cart keys/session IDs or is spreading — nothing queried the store directly or counted distinct affected carts.
What wrote the malformed payload. No change log window covering the hours before 21:56:30 was ever queried; a pre-onset cart deploy or serializer change remains unexamined.
Why checkout emits zero log lines across a 32-minute window [tr_a3d27276183e]. This may be a label mismatch or a broken shipping path, but an unlogging checkout is an unexplained second anomaly.

Whether cart's Redis instance is itself healthy at the infrastructure level — no memory, eviction, persistence or disk-capacity signal was collected, and an eviction or truncated-write condition on Redis could be the upstream producer of the bad bytes.

Whether the corruption is still being produced or is static: the identical error text suggests one bad payload replayed, but no write-path instrumentation was examined to confirm new bad writes are not occurring.

The baseline windows for both metric queries returned no samples [tr_7ba8e797a1a7, tr_6a4cad08a919], so no before/after comparison exists for either service and the prior error rate is unknown rather than zero.
The truncated 6-span failing trace with no checkout child [tr_45a6a0243e5f] is unexplained and may represent a second, distinct failure path.

alternatives.root_cause: A pre-onset cart deployment changed the protobuf schema or serializer so that newly running code cannot decode payloads written by the previous version.
alternatives.why_not: The change log records no cart deployment, though its window began at onset and did not cover the preceding hours [tr_b83043db5026], so this is not fully excluded. It is demoted because a version skew would typically fail on a schema/field-number mismatch, whereas the observed exception is specifically input ending mid-field — truncated bytes, not a misread structure [tr_871968a1ced8] — and because failures are partial rather than affecting every GetCart, which a code-wide decode incompatibility would not explain.

alternatives.root_cause: Cart's Redis backend is out of space or evicting, returning short or partial values that cart then fails to parse.
alternatives.why_not: This is a plausible producer of truncated bytes and no storage-capacity signal was ever collected, so it cannot be excluded. It is demoted because nothing in cart's own log reports a no-space or write-failure condition — the only signature is a read-side parse error [tr_871968a1ced8] — and because the cart write path (HMSET/EXPIRE) completes normally in traces [tr_45a6a0243e5f], which a full store would not permit. Even if true, the immediate fix for the unreadable entries remains the same.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no effect is expected. The mechanism identified is a malformed payload sitting in cart's Redis store: cart receives bytes successfully (HGET child span completes in 0.2-0.7ms inside failing traces [tr_45a6a0243e5f]) and fails while parsing them with an identical InvalidProtocolBufferException on every error line [tr_871968a1ced8]. The only action that addresses that mechanism is restore_data / store flush, which the brief lists as UNAVAILABLE (not built; executor performs rollback_image, revert_config and restart_service only). None of the three available actions meets its own preconditions: rollback_image requires a deploy or image change named inside the incident window, and the change log covering onset onward records none for cart [tr_b83043db5026] or checkout [tr_4ef11f576ced]; revert_config requires a configuration or flag change inside the window, and the same two queries record none; restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state, and the evidence points instead at persisted data outside the process — a cart container recreate discards cache only and would leave the bad key in Redis untouched, so the FailedPrecondition lines would resume on the first GetCart that touches it. Recommended instead: escalate to a human operator who can inspect the store directly, count distinct affected cart keys, and delete or rewrite the malformed payload.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if the malformed bytes are not persisted but are produced per-request by cart's own in-process state — for example a corrupted in-memory serializer buffer or a wedged connection multiplexer — in which case restart_service on cart would stop the error lines and the abstention cost real downtime. The observation that would show this: the FailedPrecondition line text varying across restarts or across cart replicas, or the error disappearing and reappearing without any write to the store. Current evidence argues against it — the error detail text is byte-identical across every line in the window [tr_871968a1ced8], which reads as one bad stored payload replayed rather than live corruption. It is also wrong if a pre-onset cart deploy exists: no change-log window before 21:56:30Z was ever queried [tr_b83043db5026], and if such a deploy (e.g. a serializer change) is found, rollback_image on cart would meet its preconditions and become the correct proposal. Querying change history for cart over the hours preceding 21:56:30Z is the single cheapest observation that could convert this abstention into an action.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is continued customer-visible checkout failure: cart errors ran unbroken from 21:56:30Z to the window edge at 22:02:10Z [tr_871968a1ced8] and every failing checkout aborts at its first hop, GetCart, before payment or order publish [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. Every minute without intervention is more failed multi-item checkouts. That cost is accepted deliberately, because the alternative — restarting cart on a diagnosis of persisted data corruption — destroys cart's in-process cache, is marked irreversible, resets the clock on the onset signal, and by the stated mechanism cannot remove the bad payload. A restart that appears to help would be worse than one that plainly fails: it would mask the live corruption question (nothing has yet confirmed whether bad writes are still occurring) and burn the clean onset boundary this investigation currently has.
proposal.blast_radius: No service is touched, so no caller sees a change. The population that continues to be affected is the one already affected: cart's caller checkout, and above it frontend and frontend-proxy, which re-wrap the cart status with negligible self time [tr_45a6a0243e5f]. currency, product-catalog, shipping, payment and email are never reached in failing traces and remain unaffected either way. Had restart_service been proposed on cart, the blast radius would have been cart plus connection resets seen by checkout and, transitively, frontend and frontend-proxy during the container recreate.

triage_judgement.reasoning: A critical alert on checkout with no open incidents to attribute it to and no competing signal to dismiss it. Single-seed alert gives no hint of cause yet, so fault class stays unknown.
